summary: Individual with public health surveillance experience endorses FDA's postmarket approaches and asks for owned tasks, prespecified triggers, subgroup monitoring, validated monitors and a common data specification.

Academic health system finds the risk framework and phased evaluation reasonable but wants defined axes, use-case-specific approvals, a public evaluation repository and safe-harbor adverse event reporting.

Digital mental health society backs most proposals with mental-health safeguards, rejects automatic higher risk for patient-facing use, and urges trajectory, sycophancy and crisis-response evaluation.
A commenter warns physician consensus can be wrong, urges blinded review and accredited third-party evaluators for accountability, and asks for clinical subgroup evaluation.
A psychiatric nurse practitioner says the consequence axis underweights psychiatric harm and urges mental-health adversarial testing, real-workflow monitoring, and handoff evaluation.

Nurse practitioner consultancy asks that validation include registered nurses and NPs as intended users, report human-AI team performance, and test automation bias under realistic workload.

Pediatrician urges strict premarket and postmarket rules with population-specific evidence, age-stratified pediatric data, re-evaluation after model changes outside a PCCP, and mandatory adverse event reporting.

Biopharma industry group urges risk-proportionate, system-level, lifecycle assurance of the full deployed configuration, with configuration control, purposeful human oversight and cross-Center coordination.
Nursing student supports competency-based evaluation but asks FDA to assess patient agency, equitable subgroup performance, nursing involvement and behavior under incomplete or fragmented data.
Individual asks FDA to classify each safety-critical output as data-invariant or interpretive, verifying the former against authoritative sources and benchmarking only the latter.

Postmarket monitoring firm sets conditions for trading premarket evidence for monitoring and details site-level, prespecified, independent postmarket monitoring practices.

Self-described AI agent endorses the risk framing and competency approach, and asks for externally checkable decision traces and premarket subgroup performance including neurotype.
NASS supports the framework and asks FDA to make clinical auditability and decision provenance explicit, scaled to risk, with defined professional society roles in monitoring.
RecovryAI, developing an autonomous post-operative recovery device, answers all 26 questions, tying evidence to the decisions a device makes independently and evaluating the finished system.

Commenter argues AI is unreliable and insecure for charting, and that humans must double-check everything AI says or does.

A numerical software firm urges FDA to treat doses computed by separate validated tools differently from model-generated numbers, with tool-use benchmarks and traceability.
Health professional finds AI deterioration and sepsis alerts useful but unable to detect erroneous data or patient baselines, causing alert fatigue and liability questions.
Bedside nurse asks FDA to define who oversees and can stop unsafe AI orders, include nurses, require outcome evidence, and monitor near misses.
A health professional says patients must be able to review AI-generated information before it enters their record and that AI has no place at the bedside.

Japanese digital health industry group broadly supports FDA's approach, drawing on PMDA practice, with requests for clarity, flexibility, and harmonization.
AMA supports a risk-based lifecycle approach but insists agility not lower premarket evidence, HCP oversight be proven, and manufacturers stay accountable.
Commenter raises concerns about data protection, oversight of AI updates, nurse liability for bypassing AI, and rising staffing ratios.
Clinician worries that ambient recordings cannot be turned off or kept out of the chart, harming sensitive patient conversations.
A neonatal nurse practitioner urges safeguards giving frontline clinicians authority over AI devices and preventing profit-driven misuse such as staffing cuts.
A nurse of 43 years raises concerns and asks how risk, testing with professionals, monitoring, and human sign-off will be handled.
The commenter says this should not be used in nursing and doubts it would be effective patient care.

The commenter argues nurses are excluded from AI policy, AI is inaccurate and biased, and inserting AI between nurses and patients undermines care.

A regulatory consultancy broadly supports FDA's lifecycle approach, urging workflow-level risk, effective oversight, intended-use traceability, proportionate evidence, impact-based change control, and agentic sequence testing.
A health professional states that AI use in care and records must prioritize patient safety because AI errors can cause serious harm.
ALS patient group urges a function-based risk approach, patient involvement in defining performance, representative evidence, and safeguards for connected autonomous devices.
Pathology regulatory consultant urges independent intended-use benchmarks, documented foundation models, defined change control, and reuse of foundation-model evidence across devices.
Nurse opposes AI in medical devices, citing fabrication risks, privacy concerns, and AI's inability to detect bedside equipment and assessment problems.
Health professional objects to AI recording conversations without consent and questions how verbal nuances would be handled.
Nurse questions whether AI will add error-checking burden on nurses, argues it should rely only on verified documentation, and asks how PHI will be protected.
Oncology nurses support added safeguards for patient-facing, escalation, and agentic functions and ask that nurses shape comparators and monitoring.

Regulatory advisor describes her ARCH compliance specification's per-output traceability, reverification triggers, deterministic verification gates, and model hashing as analogues for FDA's questions.
Commenter insists patient consent is required before AI is used to record them.

Device design consultancy proposes an STPA controller-based framework, crediting human review and controls only when demonstrated, instead of a licensure analogy.
Device maker answers each question briefly, favoring ties to existing standards, limited-risk treatment for clinician-reviewed functions, and FDA-defined benchmarks.
Pharma quality professional supports FDA's direction and applies validation practice: failure observability, held-out benchmarks, attributable approval, near misses, locked configurations.
Medical industry association proposes a capability-by-autonomy framework replacing FDA's activity-by-consequence axes, while broadly supporting evaluation, PCCP, and MAF proposals.

Registered nurse argues AI cannot replace nursing assessment, which depends on direct observation and body language, though it may enhance the process.
Human factors consultancy asks FDA to build explicit human factors engineering directives into each part of the framework, centering use-related risk and human-AI team performance.
A supplemental comment filed by an AI agent cites TGA, UK, and deployment evidence to argue for lifecycle monitoring and externally checkable postmarket surveillance.

BPC backs a risk-based approach but says key proposals need new congressional authority, urging user-expertise-aware risk, realistic comparators, ASCA-style third parties, sandboxes, and post-authorization PCCPs.

org: ARPA-H ADVOCATE Program and Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory
summary: ARPA-H ADVOCATE and JHU APL support FDA's lifecycle approach while asking for explicit risk modifiers, per-function autonomy limits, test coverage reports, realistic comparators, and end-to-end agent testing.

A hospice nurse reports repeated AI documentation failures and doubts AI will work in other clinical uses.
Clinician argues LLM hallucinations and transcription errors show the technology is not ready, and asks who is accountable for its errors.
Spring Health supports FDA's risk-proportionate, competency-based approach, offers its VERA-MH framework as a model, and asks for sponsor flexibility on benchmarks, thresholds, and postmarket plans.

org: Episodes of Care Solutions, Ltd. (EOCS, Ltd.)
summary: Proposes a Clinical Intelligence Assurance Framework assessing AI within real care pathways, human oversight, and patient outcomes, with coordinated monitoring across HHS agencies.

Grifols asks FDA to clarify detectability as a risk dimension, required human oversight levels, acceptance criteria for variable outputs, automatic restrictions, third-party model control, and synthetic case validation.

The Chamber wants the risk framework used for evidence, not classification, lighter premarket burdens for lower-risk devices with monitoring, workable PCCPs, voluntary confidential model sharing, and delayed agentic rules.

Lunit supports evaluating the final configured device, sponsor accountability, a voluntary confidential versioned foundation model MAF, and supplier, version, and PCCP controls for upstream model changes.
Primary care AI company urges weighing the risk of no care, lighter premarket evidence with strong postmarket safeguards, realistic comparators, and not presuming patient-facing tools higher risk.
Submission contains only the title line "Lotus Health AI Comments" with no substantive text or attachment.
Nurse opposes AI-written notes she must sign, fears replacing clinicians, and asks for independent government research before deployment.

org: Yale Collaboration for Regulatory Rigor, Integrity, and Transparency (CRRIT)

A nurse argues AI should not assess patients and must always be checked by humans.

An academic otolaryngologist calls for specialty-anchored benchmarks, field-level risk assessment, shadow deployment as confirmation evidence, model-change triggered re-benchmarking, and top risk for patient-facing diagnostics.

AI governance firm proposes a versioned device configuration record anchoring change control, foundation model change detection, reassessment triggers, supervisory agent validation, and agentic action controls.

org: Society of American Gastrointestinal and Endoscopic Surgeons (SAGES)
summary: SAGES asks FDA to cover GenAI functions that act on tissue, add action type as a risk dimension, characterize autonomy by supervision posture, and require closed-loop testing.

Individual regulatory practitioner offers draft guidance language and a demonstration script for configuration registries, evidence-gated change transitions, silent-failure monitoring, and human-authorized agent capability expansion.

Johnson & Johnson urges replacing competency determinations with intended-use performance evaluation using quantified uncertainty, and keeping risk characterization separate from classification and predicate analysis.

Family physician and CMIO supports FDA's direction, urging error detectability in risk, real-workflow confirmation, practical postmarket signals, evaluated AI monitors, and path-level agentic evaluation.
Surgeon and former CDRH office director supports the framework and proposes confirming postmarket plans can answer open questions, plus a voluntary surgical pilot of a cross-system minimum record.
A consumer wellness company supports the risk framework and competency assessment and asks for a wellness boundary, mandatory AI disclosure, designed escalation, and foundation model monitoring.
Radiation therapist urges treating patient comprehension as a risk modifier, task-based comprehension testing with representative users, and language-stratified postmarket monitoring.

Nonprofit research collective proposes replacing the two axes with probability of acting on wrong output and expected harm, mandatory robustness and subgroup benchmarks, synthetic data limits, and pinned models.
A manufacturing quality scientist urges adding input integrity to risk assessment, evaluating the configured system and guardrails, and enforcing agent boundaries deterministically.
A nurse of 48 years says these tools should be informational only, never acting without humans, and tested like any device.
A bedside nurse asks that AI be integrated cautiously without placing human clinical judgment and intuition below AI.
A perioperative nurse objects to AI replacing nurses and argues human verification of AI findings will not work in practice.

Regulatory compliance firm proposes an authorization-gated activity level, reversibility and time-to-harm dimensions, and bench-based evidence for gated functions, using dental imaging AI as its example.
Flo Health supports the two-axis framework with clearer likelihood and severity modifiers, staged real-world deployment as confirmation, and validated supervisory agents under human oversight.
Dental professional asks who sets AI standards of care and liability, and calls for AI use guidelines for dental practice.

Women's health startup asks FDA to address women explicitly: credit source traceability, judge patient tools against real alternatives, test across reproductive states, and allow privacy-preserving monitoring.
iRhythm asks FDA to distinguish bounded diagnostic deep neural networks from generative AI and keep established validation approaches for them.
Siemens Healthineers praises FDA's existing AI framework and PCCPs as a solid foundation and urges risk-proportionate oversight that supports innovation and workforce relief.

Computer engineering academic recommends criterion-level rubrics, validated LLM graders, repeated-run statistics, contamination controls, grader-version triggers, and trajectory audits for agentic devices.

org: SARA (Society for AI in Regulatory Affairs)
summary: Regulatory affairs society supports competency-based evaluation, keeping two risk axes, ground-truth comparators, validated supervisory checks, regression-test change control, and stricter agentic controls, citing EU practice.

org: Consortium for Technology & Innovation in Pediatrics (CTIP)
summary: Pediatric device accelerator supports risk-proportionate competency evaluation and flexible confirmation but warns added requirements may exclude children; urges shared pediatric evaluation resources and evidence reuse.

Academic internist supports the two-axis framework and competency model, urging detectability and reversibility modifiers, equity and adversarial testing, conversation-level risk, human-AI team comparators, and limits on postmarket trade-offs.

An informatics physician supports the risk framework and competency evaluation and proposes detectability and reversibility modifiers, subgroup and bias-language benchmarking, and adversarial simulated stress-testing.
Part 2 of a physician's comment urging conversation-level risk assessment, human-AI team confirmation against no-device care, detectability limits on postmarket trade-offs, and governed adjudicators.

Medical physicist supports competency-based evaluation but warns that agreement between AI devices and AI checkers is not independent verification.
A company supports treating foundation model updates as controlled changes, asks FDA to recognize deterministic control layers, clarify bounded PCCP changes, and test agentic behaviors.

Commenter calls the framework a solid start, endorses the two-axis matrix and premarket categories, and asks for more detailed guidance and examples.

Biostatistician suggests postmarket monitoring draw on Sentinel and BEST infrastructure, use causal inference to assess benefit or harm, and apply negative controls to diagnose bias.

Individual suggests adding patient acuity as a third risk axis, reliability as an output characteristic, and nurses and other professionals as intended users.

AGA supports the framework and competency-based approach with added risk modifiers, a three-phase evaluation pathway, limited postmarket reliance, and firm manufacturer accountability.
Qnomx proposes claim-level traceability metrics, contamination-aware genomic benchmarks, evidence of real human review, and treating evidence-corpus updates as a change category.

Device trade association urges adapting existing risk-based frameworks rather than new GenAI constructs, rejecting the two-axis model and third-party evaluators while seeking more flexible PCCPs.

org: NSF AI Research Institute on Interaction for AI Assistants (ARIA)
summary: ARIA urges evaluating conversational trajectories and patterns of use, effects on access to human support, validated simulation, postmarket reassessment, and required independent evaluation.
Heart failure titration software maker argues evidence for hybrid devices should target each generative input step, with deterministic decision logic verified conventionally.

RaySearch answers most questions, favoring risk-proportionate evidence, credit for deterministic controls, event-based reassessment, tiered change control, and clearer expectations for foundation model information.

Siemens Healthineers regulatory staff supports the concepts but asks for added risk modifiers, objective directiveness criteria, statistical benchmark rules, risk-based evidence expectations, and harmonization.
WEDI offers general AI-in-health policy tenets and asks for transparency, patient disclosure, privacy rules, adverse-event reporting, and more FDA funding, without engaging the paper's questions.
AAP asks FDA to treat pediatric developmental stage as a risk modifier throughout, test long conversations, require subgroup evidence, and substantiate human oversight.

Fault Line argues validated, independent automated benchmarking can suffice for authorization and should be rerun on live postmarket data, with performance-anchored change control.
AHA backs a flexible risk-based approach but wants the activity axis reworked, CDS tools excluded from oversight, and monitoring responsibility placed on developers.
A nurse urges FDA to include nurses in risk assessment, evaluation, and monitoring and to test whether human oversight works rather than assume it.

DiMe urges a lifecycle approach linking benchmarking to use with intended users, outcome-based patient-facing evaluation, actionable monitoring plans, and shared learning.
Ambient documentation and CDS developer urges a function-specific, risk-proportionate approach, adding detectability and oversight to risk, sponsor benchmarks, and lifecycle monitoring.

Cardiology society backs a risk-based lifecycle approach but wants added risk modifiers, demonstrated clinician oversight, limits on autonomy, rigorous patient-facing evidence, and revalidation after changes.
AI systems firm endorses the paper's approach while asking FDA to treat evaluations as tested objects, date evidence, enforce agent permissions outside models, and test oversight.

Telehealth platform urges shifting evidence burden postmarket, recognizing scalable validation as primary evidence, benchmark-based PCCPs, and lower risk credit for traceability and deterministic safeguards.

summary: Neurosurgical societies want risk judged by output reliability and decision influence, safeguards for patient-facing and generalist use, conversation-level testing, and risk-based PCCPs.

Unnamed medtech company (via counsel) supports function-based risk, continuum directiveness, PCCPs, and postmarket reliance, while seeking credit for disclaimers and safeguards and no default patient-facing uplift.

Youth digital mental health provider wants risk judged by real-world use and user vulnerability, baseline youth safeguards, credit for human oversight, proportionate change control, and shared developer responsibility.

Physician advocacy group backs a risk-based framework but wants an evidence floor, expanded risk dimensions, independent benchmarks, mandatory transparency, and strict limits on postmarket tradeoffs and PCCPs.

CHAI member consultation supports deployed-system evaluation but wants a rigorous premarket gate, layered postmarket surveillance with independent evaluators, task-specific authorization, and clear accountability.

ACR answers all 26 questions from an imaging perspective, urging demonstrated human oversight, contextual risk modifiers, non-compensatory safety thresholds, independent assessors, and bounded change control.

Kaiser Permanente supports the risk and competency framework for health-system-deployed tools but not direct-to-consumer ones, urging task-bounded authorization and clear manufacturer monitoring duties.

Patient-facing voice agent developer supports FDA's direction and proposes ten auditable minimum expectations, including independent supervisory models, clinician testing at scale, hard safety floors, and version pinning.
Tech trade association supports a flexible, risk-based lifecycle approach, asks for illustrative use cases and practical postmarket metrics, and wants agentic AI handled in a separate process.

Physician supports the risk heuristic and competency approach, adding a point-of-clinical-reliance analysis, integrated configuration testing, detection-latency limits on postmarket tradeoffs, and imaging worked examples.

The Coalition for State Sandboxes asks FDA to treat state healthcare AI sandboxes as evidence sources and partners, and to condition postmarket reliance on independent verification.

Doctronic, which operates prescription-renewal software under Utah's program, supports competency-based evaluation but asks FDA to add probability of harm, define key terms, and allow process safeguards alongside independence.

Meadows Institute urges FDA to distinguish purpose-built from general-purpose behavioral health chatbots, test full risk-response workflows with multi-turn benchmarks, and monitor both postmarket safety and clinical outcomes.

Novamigo asks FDA to create a postmarket-assured lane and time-limited evaluation period for patient-facing AI tools that log every expectation and direction, grade them against outcomes, and report error counts.
A legal scholar maps each discussion-paper approach to existing FDA statutory authority, the instrument that could carry it, and when rulemaking or legislation would be required.

Frontier Governance Group supports competency-based evaluation but asks FDA to define permissible premarket uncertainty, set a risk-proportionate evidentiary floor, and not let postmarket monitoring substitute for obtainable evidence.

Health Innovation Alliance backs the framework broadly and urges phased, monitored 'Clinical AI Confidence Compact' deployments to generate real-world evidence, no-care comparators, broader PCCPs, and liability safe harbors.

Bausch + Lomb, drawing on its Orphia eye-care patient-call agents, asks FDA to assess risk per function after verified safeguards, publish a risk-to-evidence map, avoid default prospective studies, and use envelope-based PCCPs.

Bettering Bearings asks FDA to separate task performance from conditions for responsible clinical judgment, using risk modifiers, trajectory tests, separate escalation metrics, agent authority maps, and a judgment-preservation assurance record.
Radiology report-drafting developer answers all 26 questions, backing the framework per function and shifting clinical confirmation to postmarket congruence with signed reports.
Radiology society backs a broadened risk framework and competency evaluation paired with clinical confirmation, limits postmarket tradeoffs, and stresses manufacturer accountability and transparency.
Personalized medicine coalition backs a risk-based, flexible lifecycle approach, urges risk be tied to intended use and user reviewability, and limits postmarket tradeoffs to detectable errors.
AI validation firm proposes risk axes of condition severity and reversibility, questions broad competency benchmarks, and urges local and independent evaluation plus Sentinel-style monitoring.
Health policy institute calls the approach a reasonable start, urging regulatory science research, separate synthetic-data reporting, context-specific comparators, and rigorous postmarket plans.
Hospital association supports the competency-based approach but calls the risk framework incomplete and insists manufacturers, not hospitals, carry postmarket monitoring burdens.

GI endoscopy society backs a risk-based lifecycle approach drawing on CADe experience, adding risk modifiers, specialty-anchored thresholds, bounded change control, and limits on postmarket tradeoffs.
Precision medicine AI firm seeks predictable risk-to-evidence mapping, credit for grounding and constrained outputs, realistic comparators, optional third parties, and broad class-based PCCPs.
Dental device maker supports the framework and competency approach as risk-scaled heuristics, seeks evidence mapping, envelope PCCPs, narrow supervisory agents, and agentic safeguards.
Imaging device maker urges building on ISO 14971 and existing frameworks, flexible risk-based competency evaluation, postmarket only for residual uncertainty, and evolved PCCPs.
Regulatory consultancy proposes a safety baseline for all health GenAI, classification by intended use alone, stronger postmarket focus, and harmonized foundation model disclosures.
Pathology society backs competency evaluation and third-party roles but rejects trading premarket evidence for postmarket monitoring and no-care comparators, insisting on pathologist oversight.

Academic health system supports the two-axis framework and competency evaluation but urges clear lifecycle responsibility allocation between sponsors and deployers, with stronger sponsor postmarket duties.
Small developer supports the framework, proposing modifiers, autonomy distinctions, directiveness ceilings, staged confirmation, bounded change control, and traceable, auditable outputs throughout.

Orthodontist association supports a risk-proportionate approach but insists GenAI tools operate under licensed orthodontist oversight, citing irreversible biological harms from unsupervised treatment.
Quality software vendor supports the framework and urges anchoring benchmarking, monitoring, supervisory agents, and change control in existing quality system, risk, and supplier controls.
Independent evaluator shares teen mental health benchmark results showing late-conversation failures, urging multi-turn testing, discounting disclaimers, and independent pre-deployment evaluation.

org: American Association of Physicists in Medicine (AAPM)
summary: Medical physicists' society urges an explicit evidence chain from manufacturer validation to physicist-led site commissioning and monitoring, with task-specific physics testing and bounded change control.

Imaging AI developer rejects board-exam competency inference for generative models, urges verification friction as a risk modifier, injected-error testing, and taxonomy-based continuous postmarket telemetry.
Imaging AI developer supports the framework within existing device regulation, favors proportionate evidence and domain-level validation, and opposes third-party certification that gates FDA review.
Stanford Biodesign scholars argue existing FDA tools suffice, urging function-based guidance, least burdensome evidence, voluntary third-party evaluation, and clear jurisdictional boundaries.

Swiss AI consultancy supports the framework and urges versioned configuration manifests, validated evaluation harnesses, sequestered benchmarks under independent custody, binding postmarket monitoring, and pinned models.

Device maker with retinal imaging AI supports risk-proportionate evaluation, seeking flexibility for retrospective real-world evidence, sponsor benchmarks, and comparators, and argues patient-facing delivery alone should not set risk.
AI innovator coalition argues the risk axis may misclassify devices, existing frameworks suffice, third-party evaluators add burden, and postmarket trade-offs should be sponsor-elected.
A virtual chronic-care provider asks FDA for a risk-proportionate pathway to AI patient chat and triage, with graduated autonomy, guaranteed escalation, and no-device comparators.
An emergency-care software firm endorses FDA's framework and suggests deterministic safety controls, trajectory simulation, separate escalation error reporting, and regression benchmarking.
A diagnostics manufacturer urges one SaMD-wide risk framework, existing pathways, benchmarks as supporting evidence only, IVD validation methods, bounded PCCPs, and international harmonization.
A physician-consultant proposes a seven-column risk matrix, Class II special controls, verified judges and user simulators, staged HCP review step-down, and broad PCCPs for model swaps.

A mental health venture firm supports FDA's approach and asks for patient-facing safeguards that preserve access, a clinician-supervised category, a shared crisis benchmark, and reportable-event definitions.

A testing and certification firm backs FDA's framework, adds risk modifiers, and urges benchmark governance, accredited third-party evaluation, structured lifecycle monitoring, and standard foundation model information.

CarexData supports the risk framework and competency evaluation, urging machine-reproducible benchmarks, testable guardrails, version pinning and re-execution, data provenance checks, and ISO alignment.

A physician-founder urges rule-based emergency safety layers, mandatory guideline and drug-registry grounding, PCCP updates gated by benchmarks and rollback, and preserving the non-device CDS safe harbor.
Commenter asks about patient consent, clinician liability for errors, HIPAA risks of ambient documentation, environmental costs, and protection from data breaches.
A licensed practical nurse asks for real human checkpoints before irreversible actions, user-tested explanations, prespecified postmarket degradation limits, and nursing input.
A health professional argues bedside nurses should help develop, evaluate, and implement AI tools, citing NICU monitoring and decision support as examples.

An oncology AI company supports competency-based evaluation and asks FDA to recognize biological competencies, sponsor benchmarks, tiered change control, and sponsor-controlled foundation models as lower risk.

The digital pathology association proposes a three-axis risk framework, rejects the competency framing in favor of ordinary device evidence, and asks for pathology-specific scope, change, and supply-chain clarity.

A wearable device startup asks FDA to recognize bounded device-use assistants, credit deterministic controls, reject presumed patient-facing risk, allow envelope-based PCCPs for model retirements, and keep third-party evaluation voluntary.

An individual's 131-page response keeps the two axes with bounded modifiers and sets detailed conditions for benchmarks, synthetic data, comparators, postmarket reliance, supervisors, PCCP envelopes, and agents.
Wolters Kluwer urges FDA to actively regulate only agentic GenAI functions, granting enforcement discretion to clinician-mediated tools, and doubts universal benchmarks are feasible.
Young adult patient group asks FDA to pull AI companions out of the wellness exception, rate devices by most directive function, keep premarket standards, and mandate model disclosure.

World Privacy Forum asks FDA to revise AI definitions, address privacy and consent, add inference and composition to risk assessment, require a configuration register, and use consensus-standard benchmarks.
Thermo Fisher broadly endorses the two-axis framework and competency approach, and asks for risk-based postmarket monitoring, existing change guidance, and supplier agreements on model updates.

Big Health, a GenAI device developer, asks for a likelihood risk dimension, in-session drift safeguards, joint benchmarking and clinical confirmation, credentialed-clinician comparators, and bounded PCCPs.

Hopper Healthcare supports the risk and competency approaches but asks FDA to credit validated deterministic safeguards, not presume patient-facing risk, and include conversational-infrastructure suppliers in master files.

Kestra supports FDA's risk-based lifecycle framework but asks for risk modifiers, traceability and audit expectations, separate rules for outreach agents, foundation model change governance, and AI cybersecurity controls.
Metabody AI proposes a runtime safety envelope with four routing outcomes, standardized tunable tolerance parameters, separate failure-mode metrics, and a bar set above median clinician performance.

A regulatory consultant urges FDA to tie GenAI oversight to evidence provenance, QMS design controls, lifecycle inspection readiness, validated human oversight, and trained, aligned FDA reviewers and investigators.

Endovascular robotics developer endorses the two-axis and competency approaches, drawing on autonomous-vehicle practice to support sponsor-built benchmarks, synthetic data, and accepting premarket uncertainty under conditions.

org: Program On Regulation, Therapeutics, And Law (PORTAL) and MIT Critical Data
summary: Harvard PORTAL and MIT Critical Data accept FDA's sequence but demand clinical evidence in real settings, independent experts, prespecified postmarket plans, and clarity on device jurisdiction.

org: Generation Patient (joint comment of twelve patient, clinician, and consumer organizations)
summary: Twelve patient and consumer groups urge mental-health companion guidance, reject trading premarket evidence for postmarket monitoring, and call for mandatory foundation model disclosures.
An IT director urges that safety controls, audit records, and shutdown authority be enforced and verifiable independently of the AI system they govern.

org: UCSF and UC Berkeley Center for Targeted Machine Learning and Causal Inference
summary: Two biostatisticians propose the Causal Roadmap to define evaluation estimands and comparators for GenAI device evidence.
UC Health supports FDA's deployed-product approach and proposes context modifiers, FMEA-guided testing, rolling sequestered benchmarks, staged postmarket oversight, and change-notification duties.
MetaBrain Labs describes its rules-based multi-agent context-gathering architecture and urges FDA to distinguish such systems from autonomous diagnostic agents.
Three physicians draw on a voice-AI risk Delphi to add exposure volume to risk, separate escalation errors, raise evidence for high-risk agents, and protect clinicians from shifted accountability.
Amazon backs FDA's risk- and competency-based approach, favors real-world evidence and postmarket reliance, opposes blanket clinician review, and seeks delegable postmarket duties.
Welldoc asks FDA to define small language models, multiply severity by probability on the risk axis, use hybrid deterministic AI, and add traceability and drift benchmarks.

Two quality and AI strategists argue GenAI device evidence must be tied to reproducible configurations and traceable lineage, with tiered change control, independent supervisors, and propose-then-authorize agent gates.

ACS asks FDA to address procedural surgical AI by adding context to risk, judging directiveness by effect, requiring outcome-based independent postmarket surveillance, and limiting postmarket substitution.

Anthropic broadly supports FDA's approach, urging measured credit for reviewers, whole-conversation testing, independent pivotal benchmarks, prespecified postmarket terms, and a three-event model for hosted model changes.
Statistician argues synthetic data broadens test coverage but cannot stand in for independent real-world observations; urges separate reporting, generator validation, and leakage safeguards.
Behavioral health developer asks FDA to add mental health examples, credit clinician-governed designs, allow privacy-preserving monitoring, and let PCCPs cover foundation model substitution.
Hearing aid trade group urges a risk-based approach, warns against applying GenAI rules to bounded ML, and doubts postmarket reliance given FDA's limited resources.
AI governance infrastructure firm says model-change control, postmarket reliance, and supervisory agents all depend on per-output records, model pinning, and deterministic safety layers.
Clinical AI evaluation company asks FDA to set criteria for independent, specialty-matched clinician panels that preserve disagreement across benchmarking, confirmation, and postmarket review.
California citizen asks FDA to confirm legal authority, regulate by risk, keep approval affordable, preserve patient access, mandate HIPAA-level privacy, and exclude foreign-adversary models.
Nursing informatics alliance says the two-axis framework oversimplifies risk and asks for nurse involvement, realistic workflow testing of ambient AI, and actionable postmarket surveillance.
Analytics vendor answers all 26 questions, backing the framework with added modifiers, separate synthetic data reporting, bounded PCCPs, and stronger controls for agents and supervisors.

org: Clinical Excellence Research Center, Stanford University
summary: Stanford authors argue benchmarks cannot prove control of clinical decisions and urge evaluability by design: validated primitives, physician-approved executable pathways, and verifiable action records.

org: Geisel School of Medicine at Dartmouth
summary: Therabot developers urge accepting lighter premarket evidence for correctable conversational mental health devices in exchange for layered, enforceable postmarket monitoring and process-based change control.

org: Stanford University and Johns Hopkins University (Departments of Surgery)
summary: Academic surgery researchers and clinicians support independent third parties, especially accredited evaluators performing local postmarket validation of GenAI devices in deploying hospitals.
Small patient-records software developer asks FDA to address patient-to-clinician agent exchange and to credit software-enforced controls over prompt-only controls in risk assessment.
Policy group backs the tiered framework and offers its model state law, urging service-level oversight like CLIA, a federal validator recognition pathway, and protocol-based delegation.
iBCI community asks FDA to distinguish conveying user intent from device judgment, evaluate fidelity to intent, adapt evidence to small populations, and protect neural data and continuity.

Swiss validation network supports competency-based evaluation and proposes specialty-society competency standards, independent clinician adjudication, and outcome-linked postmarket monitoring, using orthopaedic trauma as an example.
Academic researchers, drawing on an evidence review of AI scribe studies, urge a risk-specific monitoring adequacy standard before postmarket monitoring can justify greater premarket uncertainty.

Laboratory AI evaluation firm argues benchmarks need shortcut-solver controls, agentic decisions need independently checkable decision records, and adjudicators and supervisory agents must be methodologically independent.

Healthcare advising firm urges treating user training as a risk modifier, deferring patient negotiation to providers, scaling clinical confirmation to risk, PCCP drift tolerances, and institution responsibility for off-label use.

Ophthalmology society calls the two-axis framework a starting point needing added dimensions, urges context-dependent patient-facing risk, separate escalation reporting, specialist comparators, and manufacturer-accountable monitoring.

Google urges regulating only the application layer, applying CDS and wellness exclusions to GenAI, dynamic independently maintained benchmarks, a shared non-punitive safety ecosystem, and rejects master files and PCCP fit.

Pathologist opposes using commercially available generative AI in medical devices until reliable validation standards exist, citing hallucinations, poor training data, automation bias, and unclear accountability.
Psychiatric nurse practitioner supports a risk-based approach considering user, context, and consequences, with whole-conversation evaluation, balanced escalation, and patient access preserved.

org: Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence (HAI)
summary: Stanford HAI scholars call the framework a reasonable start but urge proof that human oversight works, construct-valid preregistered benchmarks, real-world testing, and enforceable prespecified postmarket plans with humans as arbiters.

Medication intelligence company argues risk depends on deployment context, asking per-context consequence scoring, a control floor for clinician-deployed patient tools, a tiered route for new uses, and a uniform safety bar.

Rare-disease patient AI developer supports evaluating the deployed device and urges log-based process measures, record faithfulness, prevalence-stratified results, safeguarded synthetic data, dual comparators, and constrained supervisory agents.

Runtime governance startup urges boundary-based intended use with deterministic enforcement outside the model, rule-deciding supervisors that fail safe, manufacturer-held policy accountability, and pinned, verified foundation models.

AI nursing company answers all 26 questions, supporting the deployed-system competency approach while urging hazard analysis beneath the axes, acuity-based escalation criteria, separate synthetic evidence, voice testing, and impact-scaled change control.

Digital health coalition broadly backs FDA's risk-based, competency-based approach while urging least-burdensome use of existing tools, voluntary third parties, flexible PCCPs, and narrow device scope.
Device law firm argues the two-axis risk framework departs from ISO 14971, the competency approach is ordinary verification and validation, and third-party reliance is risky.

Individual raises considerations for agentic devices: bounded action authority and safe resumption, system-level safety under concurrent workloads, and limiting evidence claims to what assessments support.

Connected care coalition backs a function-based, risk-proportionate approach, opposes presuming patient-facing tools high risk, and urges workflow-based evaluation, flexible evidence, and clear shared responsibilities.

Connected care coalition backs a function-based, risk-proportionate approach, opposes presuming patient-facing tools high risk, and urges workflow-based evaluation, flexible evidence, and clear shared responsibilities.

Clinical psychologist uses religious and spiritual distress to argue risk emerges across turns, urging spiritual-input reporting, separate escalation rates, corpus transparency, and agentic criteria preserving existing supports.
Wearable maker urges FDA to confirm GenAI, personalization, and conversation do not by themselves turn general wellness functions into devices or raise their risk.
AI company argues GenAI devices should be bounded by independently enforced, verified deterministic controls, with probability of harm added to FDA's framework and agentic authority tightly limited.

AI psychiatry clinic endorses the risk framework and competency approach, urging published stage gates for graduating autonomy, standard-of-care evaluation, sandbox evidence credit, and flexible change control.

Informatics association urges probability-and-severity risk tiers with contextual modifiers, trajectory testing, standard-of-care comparators, limited postmarket tradeoffs, bounded PCCPs, and standardized AI exposure data.
AI company warns aggregate performance can hide patient-level risk and that low-risk functions become consequential through reliance and workflow chains, urging FDA to examine these questions.

Regulatory validation firm says competency evaluation needs a standardized benchmarking and adjudication record, validated benchmarks, independent adjudicators including LLM judges, and validated supervisory agents.

A device regulatory reviewer answers all 26 questions, urging FDA to anchor the approach in existing ISO/IEC standards, test whole conversations and configurations, and keep synthetic data out of validation evidence.

A clinical AI safety evaluation firm answers all 26 questions, favoring high-volume trajectory testing, recurring re-benchmarking, reproducible non-LLM evaluators, and open participation by independent for-profit evaluators.

A software company argues GenAI risk must be assessed as an integrated workflow system through hazard-level likelihood and severity analysis, with site-level validation, phased postmarket pilots, and contractual model controls.

A device developer supports FDA's direction but urges evaluating outputs by the clinical actions they produce, keeping statistical rigor, using reference-standard comparators, and allowing staged autonomy under PCCPs.

An independent healthcare AI evaluator urges interactive environment-based testing, clinician rubrics where critical errors fail outright, rotating held-out benchmarks, and a defined role for independent evaluators.

A regulatory consultancy urges a technology-neutral, least-burdensome approach built on existing guidance, equal weight for automation benefits, less PCCP prespecification, and meaningful reliance on certified third parties.

org: Loma Linda University School of Medicine (students)
summary: Medical students answer Q7 to Q26, backing risk-scaled competency evaluation with real-world testing, independent review for high-risk devices, supplementary synthetic data, and clinician approval for agentic actions.

A regulatory-intelligence firm supports FDA's architecture and offers operational tools: configuration bills of materials, risk modifiers, a directiveness ladder, entrustable activities, safety floors, and envelope-based PCCPs.

A digital therapeutics maker proposes a Bounded Generation Specification, GenAI expansions from a validated clinical baseline without new trials, an agentic therapeutics pathway, and rules for devices inside AI platforms.

A radiologist reports undetected sensitivity decline in a cleared PE triage algorithm and asks for fixed-cadence performance thresholds, manufacturer duties on site signals, and a no-determination output.

A former FDA adverse-event expert urges fixing device identification, version-level traceability, adverse event coding transparency, and dependency management before expanding GenAI device regulation.
Commenter endorses risk- and use-based benchmark selection, asks for aligned benchmarking across lifecycle stages, and calls for independent benchmark maintainers and evaluators.
